1363711043726417920.a:
A far cry from the satellite station I built around 1994. I used a Yaesu FT-401B (bottom right) vacuum tube based transceiver to uplink and I used the President HR-2510 (upper left) to receive the downlink. Sputniks RS-10/11 and 12/13 were aboard COSMOS spacecraft on 21/29 MHz. Tweet by @DavidLNorris t.co

https://x.com/DavidLNorris/status/1363705993411100672

1363711046419120128.a: Russian HF transponders were worldwide many days. Since the HF signals bounce around the ionosphere you would often get multipath and hear yourself echoing on the downlink as it received your signal from many loops around the Earth. Light time around Earth is 1/7th second.

1363713941340377090.a: Worth noting the analog TV was useful for the Nintendo and cable TV. However, the smaller coax on the metal plate lets me switch the TV to an outdoor antenna. During bad weather the local police post had weather RADAR transmitting on 439.25 MHz which was close to a cable channel.

1363713942611255302.a: The burgundy and tan box on top of the FT-401B with the compass rose is the antenna rotator control. The 29 Mhz antenna was a 2 element 29 MHz Yagi made from 4 trimmed CB (27 MHz) fiberglass whips angled skyward slightly. The tilt helped when the satellite was directly overhead.

1363714470984450051.a: And, yes, I cringe looking at the bends on the coax I used to do back then. However HF doesn´t much care. I think I was using mostly Belden 9913 and some 8214 cable. TV cable was quad shield RG-6 satellite TV coax.
